questions.q: Why does this lesson say experienced developers looking things up constantly is not a sign of weak knowledge?
options: Because it is a sign of correctly prioritizing accuracy over guessing, rather than memorizing every method signature in advance
Because experienced developers are required by their employers to look everything up
Because documentation is only useful for complete beginners
Because Apex changes its syntax every single day
questions.explain: The lesson frames frequent lookups as correctly prioritizing accuracy over guesswork -- a habit of effective programming, not a gap in knowledge.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does the Apex Developer Guide on developer.salesforce.com matter as the authoritative source, compared to a five-year-old blog post?
options: Blog posts are always factually wrong
The official guide reflects the actual current behavior of the actual current platform, while an older post might describe something since changed, deprecated, or that never worked as claimed
The Apex Developer Guide is the only place Apex code can legally be written
Blog posts cannot be read by beginners
questions.explain: The lesson's reasoning is specifically about currency and accuracy: official docs track the platform's real current behavior, while third-party content can describe outdated or incorrect behavior, even though it's still useful for examples and context.

questions.q: Given the error message 'Line: 4, Column: 20 — Variable does not exist: discountRate', what does this lesson say you should check first?
options: Immediately search a Stack Exchange post titled 'my code is broken'
Rewrite the entire program from scratch
Look at line 4 specifically, and check spelling and whether discountRate was actually declared in a scope visible from that line
Ignore the line number, since it is rarely accurate
questions.explain: The lesson's systematic approach says to find the referenced line number and check what the message actually claims against the code -- for 'Variable does not exist,' that means checking spelling and scope, directly connecting back to Lesson 7's scope concept.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend searching the exact error text in quotes rather than a vague paraphrase?
options: Because quoted searches are required by Salesforce's terms of service
Because a literal search like "Variable does not exist" is far more useful at finding the specific, relevant problem than a vague search like "my code is broken"
Because vague searches always return zero results
Because the exact error text is never actually helpful
questions.explain: The lesson's fourth step explicitly contrasts searching the exact error text in quotes against a vague paraphrase, favoring the precise search as the faster path to a relevant answer.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the organization of the Apex Developer Guide?
options: Entirely alphabetically with no other structure
Organized by language concept (data types, collections, classes) and by specific class reference documenting exact method signatures and behavior
Only as a single long unindexed page
Organized exclusively by error message text
questions.explain: The lesson describes the guide as organized both by language concept and by specific class reference with exact signatures and behavior -- the structure worth getting comfortable navigating before the Apex-specific courses later in this path.
